The Cut-throat finch (Amadina fasciata) hatches from eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] after a developmental period of roughly 12.5 days [ab = roughly 12.5 days], a duration that aligns with the incubation schedules observed in other estrildid finches of comparable egg size. Newly emerged chicks are notably altricial, possessing a minimal initial wet body mass of only 1.6 grams [Ww0 = 1.6 grams] at the moment of hatching. This modest starting weight, typical of passerine nestlings that rely heavily on parental provisioning, necessitates a period of intense growth and care within the nest. The nestling phase progresses rapidly, with individuals achieving the capacity for sustained flight after 22 days since hatching [tx = 22 days since hatching], a milestone that marks the transition to fledging under optimal thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Throughout this early ontogeny, the developing chicks are entirely dependent on their parents for both thermoregulation and nutrient delivery.

During the period of active development and metabolic activity, typically occurring at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledglings continue to refine their flight skills and foraging abilities while still receiving occasional food from the adults. The onset of sexual maturation follows a distinct schedule, with puberty occurring at 66 days since hatching [tp = 66 days since hatching] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The subadult plumage gradually gives way to the characteristic adult coloration, particularly the striking red throat patch that gives the species its common name. Young birds that have completed their post-juvenile moult closely resemble adults but may be distinguished by subtle differences in feather wear and the intensity of their facial markings. During this phase, individuals begin to form loose foraging flocks and explore potential breeding territories, although full reproductive capability is not yet achieved. The social dynamics within these juvenile groups likely play a role in establishing future pair bonds and dominance hierarchies among the population.

First breeding attempts in the Cut-throat finch occur after a period of maturation, with the initial brood produced at 365 days since hatching [tR = 365 days since hatching] when maintained at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Reproductive output is modest compared to many other passerines; females typically lay a clutch consisting of 5 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch consisting of 5 eggs] per nesting attempt and produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. This constrained breeding strategy may be linked to the unpredictability of resources in their native semi-arid savanna habitats. Nesting pairs construct dome-shaped grass structures in thorny shrubs or tree hollows, providing protection from predators and the intense subtropical sun. The incubation duties are shared between both parents, a common trait among estrildids that enhances egg survival during the 12.5 day incubation period. The timing of breeding is closely tied to rainfall patterns, ensuring that the dependent nestlings have access to abundant grass seeds and insects.

Adult females attain a maximum body mass of 17.8 grams [Wwi = 17.8 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic weight typical of healthy, reproductively active individuals in the population. This ultimate wet weight is reached after the completion of skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Males tend to be slightly more diminutive, rarely exceeding 16 grams, though the difference is not as pronounced as in some other finch species with stronger sexual dimorphism. Basal metabolic rate measurements taken from resting birds under post-absorptive conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] indicate a maximum oxygen consumption of 38.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 38.5 milliliters per hour], a rate that is consistent with the allometric scaling predictions for a passerine of this body mass. The high metabolic demands of maintaining a 41.6 °C body temperature are met through a diet dominated by small, hard seeds that are hulled using the bird's stout conical bill. Water conservation is efficient, allowing the species to persist in arid environments where free-standing water is scarce for much of the year.

Recorded maximum longevity in the wild for the Cut-throat finch reaches 3102 days [am = 3102 days], a lifespan equivalent to roughly 8.5 years that is maintained under ambient conditions near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, compared to some northern hemisphere finches of similar size, may reflect the lower extrinsic mortality pressures typical of stable tropical and subtropical environments. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in feather quality and reproductive output. The species is a cooperative breeder on occasion, with helpers at the nest assisting the breeding pair in feeding the altricial young, a behavior that may buffer against the high energy costs of chick rearing and contribute to adult survival. Parasite loads, particularly from ectoparasitic mites and avian pox virus, can cause notable mortality in some populations. The Cut-throat finch remains a common resident across much of sub-Saharan Africa, where its adaptability to both natural and human-modified landscapes has allowed it to persist successfully in a variety of dry woodland and scrub habitats.
